data.title: Erythrasma — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erythrasma** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define erythrasma.**
- Chronic superficial infection of the stratum corneum by Corynebacterium minutissimum (Gram-positive diphtheroid) in body folds

**Q2. Clinical types?**
- Interdigital (commonest — 4th toe web; maceration, scaling, fissuring)
- Intertriginous/flexural (groin, axillae, submammary, intergluteal) — sharply marginated reddish-brown, finely scaling, slightly wrinkled patches; mild or no itch
- Generalised/disciform (rare; trunk, in diabetics)

**Q3. Predisposing factors?**
- Diabetes, obesity, hyperhidrosis, warm humid climate, poor hygiene, advanced age, immunosuppression

**Q4. What is the key bedside test?**
- Wood's lamp: coral-red fluorescence from porphyrins (coproporphyrin III) produced by the organism
- Recent washing removes porphyrins → false negative; ask patient not to wash for a day

**Q5. Differentiate erythrasma from tinea cruris.**
- Tinea: active raised scaly border with central clearing, itchy, KOH shows hyphae, no coral-red fluorescence
- Erythrasma: uniform brown patch without active edge, not very itchy, coral-red fluorescence, KOH negative, Gram stain shows rods/filaments
- Both may coexist (interdigital 'complex' with Candida)

**Q6. Other differentials?**
- Candidal intertrigo (satellite pustules), inverse psoriasis (glazed red, no scale), seborrhoeic dermatitis, pityriasis versicolor, Hailey–Hailey disease, acanthosis nigricans

**Q7. Treatment?**
- Topical: fusidic acid, clindamycin, erythromycin, mupirocin, or azoles (miconazole, clotrimazole — also cover fungi and Candida), benzoyl peroxide wash
- Oral: erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 14 days or clarithromycin 1 g single dose for widespread disease
- Prevent: keep folds dry, loose cotton clothes, weight loss, antibacterial soap, control diabetes

**Q8. Which other diseases show fluorescence under Wood's lamp?**
- Tinea capitis — Microsporum: bright green; favus (T. schoenleinii): dull green
- Pityriasis versicolor: yellow-green/golden
- Pseudomonas: green; pitted keratolysis/trichomycosis: coral red/none
- Porphyria cutanea tarda: pink-red urine fluorescence; vitiligo: chalk-white accentuation
- Erythrasma: coral-red

**Q9. What is trichomycosis axillaris?**
- Corynebacterium (C. tenuis) concretions on axillary/pubic hairs — yellow, red or black nodules on the hair shaft; sweat may be coloured; shave and topical antibiotics/benzoyl peroxide

**Q10. Describe the organism and its fluorescence.**
- Corynebacterium minutissimum — Gram-positive, non-spore-forming diphtheroid rod (lipophilic); produces coproporphyrin III which fluoresces coral-red under Wood's lamp (washed off by bathing)

**Q11. Interdigital erythrasma — features and complex.**
- Commonest form — macerated white scaling and fissuring in 3rd/4th toe webs, often with dermatophytes, Candida and Gram-negative bacteria ('dermatophytosis complex'); treat with topical azoles (cover all organisms) and keep webs dry

**Q12. Histopathology/ Gram stain findings.**
- Gram stain of scrapings: Gram-positive rods/ filaments in stratum corneum; histology rarely needed — organisms in upper stratum corneum on PAS/ Gram stain, minimal inflammation

**Q13. Erythrasma and diabetes — significance.**
- Disciform/ generalised erythrasma is commoner in diabetics and obese — screen blood sugar in extensive or recurrent disease

**Q14. Systemic treatment doses.**
- Erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 14 days, or single-dose clarithromycin 1 g; tetracyclines alternative; topical fusidic acid/ clindamycin/ erythromycin/ azoles for localised

**Q15. Prevention of recurrence.**
- Keep folds dry, loose cotton clothing, antibacterial soap washes, absorbent powders, weight loss, control diabetes, treat hyperhidrosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Coral-red fluorescence in the groin — erythrasma
- Most common site: 4th toe web

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
